inline.s: To He Jinwu

I recall how the ancients spoke of men whose hair turned white together yet who remained as strangers, and of men who met for the first time beneath a tilted carriage canopy and were as old friends. Indeed there are those with whom no word is spoken and yet the Way abides of itself. But when it comes to the hour of calamity and of life and death, to look about for one who understands the heart without a word, even amid bonds and fetters — such a one is rare indeed. Why? Because men are readily moved in the mind that knows, but kindness is hard to bestow where it can never be repaid.

In former days, for my own misconduct, I brought down the emperor's wrath and was delivered to the provincial judge for interrogation. Thunder rolled above me, and cauldrons stood before me, so that my clear and steadfast heart could find no way to make itself known. You, sir, holding your commission, oversaw the punishment, and yet you lingered and hesitated amidst the rods and lashes. Even had my body been of metal and stone, how could it have borne that furnace and bellows? Yet by good fortune I relied on a single word from you, and the matter was settled. Truly it was as if copious rain had been showered upon a blazing fire, as if sweet dew had been poured into parched entrails; at once my whole being was cooled and I brightened into life, and I did not even know that I was amid knives and saws.

The law of the court, three cubits long, showed me no slightest leniency. Yet as I looked aside I saw your unwillingness to harm, rising plainly in your brow and eyes, and I knew well that you were a man of benevolence and a noble gentleman. I could only engrave my gratitude upon my heart, not knowing whose son you were. Now I have gone deep into the land of miasma, at the tail end of famine, on the brink of nine deaths, and my thoughts of your lofty righteousness have never once left my breast. Not long ago I asked a colleague of yours, and so learned that you are Master He. I respectfully write this brief letter to lay before you the private feelings of one who cherishes your virtue.
Reply to Zheng Kunya, Grand Coordinator

From afar you have graciously let the white-hair light shine eastward over ten thousand and eight thousand lands; and in that radiance the ascetic of austerities seems to stand before me, so that I bow to your compassionate countenance as if in person and hear the wondrous meaning with my own ears. Again I have been sprinkled with sweet dew, and the dust of habit is suddenly emptied away. The joy that leaps in my breast cannot be conveyed in words.

I have heard that the wondrous practice of the bodhisattva lies in testing the mind in every circumstance one meets. Where afflictions are emptied, there is no need to seek prajñā elsewhere; where the dusts are penetrated, just this is the gate of mystery. As I recite and revere that one phrase, the Ultimate Reality, it is truly a golden lancet for a film-covered eye. I have received in person your vow, though the hour for bowing at your feet has not yet come. Deluded feelings cling and cling, and my admiration only deepens. I only pray that true compassion will gather me in and not forsake the one who has affinity. When the wind is fair, I hope all the more that you will let down a hand from afar. This is what I thirst for.

Wuyang has long been called a land of the uncouth; the walled barracks where I dwell are no monastery. I rely on the sacred compassion and take ten thousand li as my taming and discipline, working cautiously at the forge and hammer. Fortunately I purge poison with poison, and my mean and narrow habits seem gradually to melt away. Truly it is like drinking water: only the drinker knows the warmth or chill. Yet in the end I am still like a fish on dry land blowing froth.

Caoxi in Lingnan is the place where the Sixth Patriarch unfolded his teaching, the Zhu and Si of the Chan gate; his flesh body is still there. I venture to wish to carry one handful of earth to seek blessing in the stillness and light, quietly dissolving old karma. From the first I have not dared to slacken body and mind, only fearing to fall out of step; from time to time I come and go amid the ranks. Now, relying on the indulgence of the authorities, it seems I may rest my shoulders.

Recently, while begging for food at Lingjiang, I suddenly received your jade-like letter descending from heaven like the sound of a celestial drum. Three times over I recited your compassionate intent: truly it is boundless great compassion, which does not forsake those with affinity even in a mote of dust or a pore of the skin. That one phrase about the hidden and the hidden hunter is truly a needle thrust into the sore place. Gratitude suffuses my heart, and I bow in thanks beyond measure.

You instruct me to settle my mind wherever I am; this is precisely liberation in every mote of dust. I pray you will skillfully tame and subdue, to widen the ship of deliverance. This is my utmost hope.
Reply to Ge Zixiu

From your letter I learn that even as a child you knew to ask yourself what the mind is: you took the lump of flesh to be the mind, and yet when the body still lies there after death, why is it no longer aware? At these few words about seeking the mind and not finding it, I could not help exclaiming in astonishment again and again. Since I entered the Dharma and turned toward the Way, and went into the mountains to practice, more than thirty years have now passed; yet among the black-robed and white-robed I have met in all the land, among those who first set their minds on the Way, I have never seen anyone make such a discovery of the novice's mind as this. The reason is that the buddha-nature of all living beings is the same, but the conditions of prajñā carried from former habits differ in depth, and the seeds of hearing and perfuming received from the good teachers one has drawn near in many lives differ in being false or true, sudden or gradual; hence the resolve to enter the Way differs in being crooked or straight, sincere or feigned, slow or swift.

What you describe all comes from having drawn near true and genuine teachers in many lives and from the unsurpassed prajñā seed of hearing and perfuming: the habit-energy has issued from within, and so from childhood you spoke it out unawares. Moreover, this seed is deep-rooted, and so it presses and presses, lying across your breast, lodged and blocked so that you cannot set it down even for a moment. Therefore you cannot swallow it and cannot spit it out, very much like an object stuck in your chest, only you cannot find it. Because you take it for an object, you cannot find it; and all your life your thoughts and deliberations cannot believe in themselves or decide themselves, so whenever you meet someone you go searching for it in him. When you are shown empty space, you take it as empty space; when you hear a shout, you take it as a shout. Yet empty space is form and a shout is sound; because in many lives you have flowed and turned in sound and form and grown practiced in it, you are now carried off by it again. And the reason you are carried off is only that you take this mind as an object and take sound and form as sound and form; hence in daily use, seeing form and hearing sound, you set them up as enemies of the mind. This is precisely what is called seeking Chang'an from inside the Hanyuan Hall: how could you ever escape the cage?

Have you not heard the ancients say: call it a thing and it is already missed? Again they said: never seek it from another; far, far it grows distant from me. Again: seeing form is not to be concerned with form; hearing sound, it is not sound. Again: in the place of sound, hearing is complete; outside seeing, there are no dharmas. Sayings such as these can kill a man, and they can also bring him to life; broadly speaking, they kill the living and bring the dead to life.

You say of yourself that the mind cannot be found. This is the most intimate point of all. Why will you not believe your own mind, but instead give rise to all sorts of thoughts and seek elsewhere? Have you not heard how, when Bodhidharma sat facing the wall, the Second Patriarch Shenguang said, My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify it. Bodhidharma said, Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you. After a long while Shenguang said, Seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable. Bodhidharma said, I have pacified your mind for you. From then on this saying spread through the world, and was called the single transmission and direct pointing. From the Sixth Patriarch down through Nanyue and Qingyuan to the five houses and the seventeen hundred koans, throughout heaven and across the earth, those who spoke of Chan and spoke of the Way and brought life and death to an end cannot be counted. All of them come from Shenguang's one phrase, seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable.

If you insist that the mind is an object that can be sought from others and that teacher and disciple can hand to one another, then look: what object did Bodhidharma hand to Shenguang with his own hand, and what did he receive with his own hand? And when men look at Shenguang's phrase, seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable, it is the same as your own words; why was Shenguang right, and why do you not believe? If you say your aspiration differs from Shenguang's, then the buddha-nature of living beings must differ too; if it is not different from Shenguang's, why was Shenguang free of doubt while you doubt the more? If you say that this very unfindability is itself awakening, why did Shenguang awaken once and awaken forever, while you, after hearing the shout, said that the knot of doubt had gone you knew not where, and yet today you are still not through the ancestral koans, and the words have become a further obstruction?

Just look and see where the fault lies. In the very moment when the shout of no-thought was truly heard, how did the knot of doubt suddenly fall away? What did you see that made you so free and easy? Why are you not free and easy today? Look at the place where you are not free and easy — who is it that binds you? At the place where the text does not open — who is it that obstructs you? You need only put forth your strength; drill right at the sore spot. When you have drilled to the place where there is no place left to land, suddenly you will see through it with your own eyes, and only then will you believe that this mind is not a thing and needs no seeking outside. Only then will you know that all your former error was error to the very end, and that this no-error is no-error to the very end. At such a time you will believe that what I say today is very much like raising the voice to stop an echo, or painting legs on a snake. Since words cannot reach the meaning, I have written carelessly as the brush ran, and unwittingly the rattan vines have spread over all the ground. When you have read it, spit it out and burn it; and do not leave it for later men, to make of it a topic that breeds fresh knots of doubt.
To Hu Shun'an, Censor

As for your plan of returning east, I know your courage and loyalty; there can be no miscalculation in it. This too is my humble wish. But the fortune and emolument of a life are all fixed beforehand from former lives; how can man prevail over Heaven? If by some chance it cannot be so, how can one then sit and wait for liberation before one may advance in the Way? Even now, outwardly seated among the carriages and caps of office, inwardly harboring the Buddha's mind, when you meet things and face occasions, rousing kindness and exercising compassion, then all that meets your eye is a seed of buddhahood and a field of blessing without end. If you but give it a little attention, the merit you make in a single day of leisure will be a thousand and ten thousand times greater than that trivial effort. Moreover, your authority is like heaven and earth; life and death lie in your hands. The springs of good and evil you can surely perceive clearly, and the subtlest turnings of events hang upon it in the greatest degree. The strategy of planning and of bringing peace to the realm is, within your great wisdom, no more than a glance.

Only take compassion as the root and use compassion to aid others; practice skillful means widely, and take your ease within the great samādhi. This is to manifest the body of a magistrate and perform the Buddha's work. How can such a man be spoken of in the same breath as one who seeks only the glory of a single body? By means of these very fetters you will turn them into a vehicle for victory. Why then be so anxious, hiding your traces and fleeing from form, while you sit and let the days and months gallop by? A thousand li away in thought, I have nothing to offer you; I take this stale talk to provoke a spit from you. What do you say?

All my life my one thought has been to bring life and death to an end directly. For more than twenty years, if I set my will on the mountains and forests, then even if I cannot penetrate to full realization and match the ancients, still at the crucial juncture of life and death I have good reason to trust: all demonic foes are in the end bodhi, adorning the fruit of buddhahood. As for other calamities and gains and losses, right and wrong, blame and praise, I leave them to nature. Why then strive to be at peace? Therefore since the day I fell into trouble, this single thought of a cool mind and ground has not shifted even for a moment. From last winter in the tenth month, I set my horse's head southward from Jicheng, through bone-piercing ice and snow, and in the twelfth month reached Baixia, where I met my old mother on the river and took joyful leave of her. On the eighth day I raised sail and went west. What I rely on is that feeling is withered and wisdom exhausted, the phantom shadow wholly dissolved, a bright mirror and still water, by which I may amuse myself. This stretch of karmic circumstance has been forged and tempered in the great furnace; do not let it entangle your heart on my account. I only wish you to quietly nourish the harmony of Heaven and await the highest joy. If Heaven grants me to return alive, I still hope to finish the unfinished karma between us and keep you company in my remaining years.

Since I fell into trouble, I have truly been at the brink of nine deaths; yet looking at it now with the true eye, I do not see the slightest mark of movement or stillness. Though ten thousand li lie between us, in truth we are not apart by so much as a half-step. I think of how you and I forgot all forms for half a lifetime; surely you have long since entered this Dharma gate, so how could you fall back into the common way, galloping in thoughts of coming and going, and wearing a dreamlike look of grief? This circumstance of mine not only surpasses thirty years of pilgrimage, it is enough to surpass the practice of vast kalpas. In Leiyang the heat steams like a cauldron, and those who die of miasma lie thick as on a scorched marsh. I sit alone in the charnel ground, drinking the miasmic smoke as if it were sweet dew, enduring hunger and emptiness as if filled with fine ghee. Were it not that feeling is withered and wisdom exhausted, how could I savor it? Recently I have gained the Great General as a protector of the Dharma, and have borrowed a branch among the walled barracks of the provincial capital. In the leisure left from bearing arms I sit withered behind a closed door; all conditions are suddenly cut off, and I read only the Laṅkāvatāra, inquiring into the mind-seal that came from the West and finishing the koans not yet finished. That the goodness of merit and the vajra mind have already become a banner of light — surely I am not unworthy of the gate and wall. The ancients once said that when the ancestors are not clear, the calamity reaches the sons and grandsons. My good fortune is that I have not fallen into that saying. The Buddha said that to give away seven treasures enough to fill the Ganges' sands is not equal to upholding four lines of this sūtra. Knowing that you do not forget the poor child, I venture this to comfort you. What else is there to say?

I sit amid the barbarian smoke and miasmic fog, and I am glad that the conditions for living grow daily thinner and the conditions for the Way grow daily thicker. The more the body suffers, the happier the mind. Then what place is not the sovereign's grace, and what thing is not the Buddha's power? This may be spoken to one who knows me; it is hard to speak of to common men. How is your Dharma body, I wonder. Vimalakīrti has said: would you know how to rid yourself of old age and sickness? There is only the study of the unborn. And a hundred years of light and shadow pass as between pinched fingers — how much can there be? Your years, sir, are daily higher and the prospect before you daily narrower. The flavors of this turbid world you have tasted all but to the dregs. As the proverb says: in the end salt is this salty and vinegar this sour — and to what end does it all come? The ancients said: when you come it is all very well; I fear only that when you go it will not be as when you came. This is no empty saying.

Think carefully, sir. Your former fame and career, together with your plans for sons and daughters — all are another man's business. What is your own business? If a single thought is sharply awakened to this, you will cry out unawares, and of yourself grow urgent, and set your own feet in order for the great matter of life and death. If you do not grow urgent and set it in order, then you have still not sharply awakened; and if you do not awaken once, sharply, then you are greatly not the man I take you for. Such is the business of a hero and true man. Twenty years ago I already knew that you would speak of this one thing, and so I did not spare body or life but wished to walk with you. But though half of it is piling up hidden merit and half is nourishing the body, and so we muddle on to today, yet within it there is one small red heart, very much like Zhang Liang's resolve to be for Han from first to last. For more than ten years I have talked and laughed with you — all of it a realm of empty bloom, mere human sentiment and Buddhist business; in truth we never once broke open liver and gallbladder together. Yet with you I have a single inch of heart and intestine that shines clear and mirrors clear, and you have never failed to know this inward song of mine. I had hoped we would return together with white heads and finish this matter together. How could it be that in a single morning we are torn apart and scattered even to this? From this very thing one may contemplate life and death. And now, though we dwell within the same heaven and earth, and though ten thousand li divide us, seen with the heavenly eye we are still next-door neighbors; yet we cannot once receive your countenance and take in your color and be glad as in former days. How much less along the long road of life and death, once parted into the dark and distant, when shall we meet again? If I cannot return alive, then it is a long farewell from you; and when I put forth another head, I do not know whether it can be as in this life and on this day. To speak of it brings great grief and bitterness. I have received from you the righteousness of one who knows me; without this I cannot repay you. And if you believe that I have not come to this place, then again I have no way to answer one who knows me.
To Zhou Lizhai, Court Historian

Formerly, though in my heart I secretly admired your noble forbearance, I never had the chance for deep speech. Yesterday, carrying my bowl into the royal city, I was fortunate to meet you beneath the dragon-flower tree; seeing how genuine and pure your resolve for the Way is, my joy penetrated to the very seat of my heart. The ancients made light of a thousand pieces of gold and heavy a single promise; a true scholar values only one who knows him. Henceforth I, a mountain monk, shall give my whole life to the mountains and seas, and covet nothing else. Since your Dharma eye is perfect and bright, how could you ever again fault the blind and blear-eyed? I privately think that the literary fortune of the East begins with you, and that the fortune of the Dharma may perhaps belong to this unworthy man. Worldly and world-transcending are of mutual use to each other; this too is a strange thing between the two realms. This is no mad speech; it is truly what I hope for from you, that you would take the Way as your own weight.
Reply to the Zhou Brothers, Ziyin and His Elder

In the world, gathering and scattering, arising and ceasing, formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness — in the conditioned dharmas this is the way of things, and what is there in it to grieve over? What is truly grievable is that in the long night of darkness this torch of wisdom should be lost, so that the sons of the Buddha have nowhere to turn for refuge, and the seeds of wisdom and the sprouting seedlings of the spirit are daily scorched and withered by the blazing flames of the five desires, unable to come to the perfect fruit of victory. The six dusts darken the heaven of the nature; the weeds of craving lay waste the ground of the mind; afflictions blot out the grove of merit; greed and anger storm the house of nirvāṇa; they fell it with the axe of wine and lust and let it be trampled by the monkey and the horse, until day by day it lies waste and at last becomes a wild tangle.

I pray that in thought after thought, mind after mind, you will take this to heart with sorrow, and nourish and cultivate, weed and tend it, guard and fence it round, so that the flower of awakening spreads fresh and you adorn the jeweled ground. I hope that all gods and men may each harbor the seed of wisdom, and that creeping things and wriggling things and all that lift their heads may together ascend the shore of awakening. Thus you will not only raise your family's name through all ages, but will be enough to wash away the shame of the Dharma gate today. Without this, what hope could I place in you and your brother? On a journey of ten thousand li, if you take this to heart, we are still neighbors.
To Jiao Congwu, Court Historian

I reflect that in this age of the Dharma's decline, when all is thin and few, the dragons and gods have pushed you forward to manifest the body of a magistrate and raise the great banner of Dharma, to serve as the eye of gods and men in this age. This is no small matter. We were parted for many years, and yesterday we met beneath the tree, as if in another life. A human life drifts on and on, and is as dreamlike as this. And when I behold your countenance of the Way and your heavenly form, truly you are one who, without rising from the samādhi of cessation, manifests all manner of dignified conduct. Were it not that the light of your mind secretly returns, how could it illumine so perfectly? How could it be measured by sound, voice, form, and appearance? My joy is beyond measure.

I am ashamed that my faculties are dull and inferior; for twenty years I have worn my heart out in the mountains and forests, and still I sit atop the pole, with nowhere at all to let go. Yet the cause of the great matter is truly not easy. At parting I received one word of instruction from you, and my gratitude is boundless. Returning, I sat stiff and still in a hollow cliff, mind after mind shining alone; how dare I fail one who knows me? At times the sea is limpid and the sky clear, and the Dharma body suddenly appears — is this not the meeting of stimulus and response?

In my leisure I have opened the Zhuangzi with its wings and found that it gathers the great achievements of the various schools. Though the commentaries are often severe, every man has his own Zhuangzi; it is not Zhuangzi's own Zhuangzi. Only you have entered this samādhi very deeply — why not overturn it completely? I have often argued this: Laozi came forth in an age without a Buddha, and I would venture to class him with the pratyekabuddhas. As for Zhuangzi, he has not forgotten attachment to dharmas; he enters into play with spiritual powers, and his transformations are many, dazzling men's eyes. Unless one walks arm in arm with him, few escape being toyed with by him. But if you see through to the bottom, there truly is a separate gate of liberation. In the ten thousand ages below, this old man may be called your meeting at dawn and dusk. In my former pilgrimage I took these two old men as companions, and constantly observed their movements; there was much that hit the mark in my heart, though it is hard to describe in words. In the Inner Chapters I once marked a few words, but have not yet copied them out; in time I shall ask for your correction.
To Yang Fusuo, Junior Minister

Reading your preface to the Comprehensive Record of Caoxi, every word flows out from the true mind of great compassion. All who see or hear it are filled with great joy; how much more, a thousand years hence, will it awaken how many men from their dreams? Our Patriarch Lu, in the great samādhi of stillness, must surely appear with a serene and joyful countenance, palms joined in praise. When Master Huang came, I again received your Dharma words; and you say that there is still something not quite at ease, though your praise of this mountain rustic seems already excessive. Only Lord Haimen is one who has entered the inner chamber of Caoxi; I venture to beg one word from him, to add yet more to the flame.
Reply to Zai, Supervising Secretary

You have set before me the teaching of cause and effect. It is perfectly clear and admits no doubt; there is not the least discrepancy. It is what is called shadow and echo. But as to your earlier teaching about evil men, this principle is the most hidden and hard to understand, and yet it is also easily believed as certain.

Only the mind of a sage is perfectly luminous: looking back, it sees no beginning; looking forward, it sees no end. Like a great perfect mirror, it illumines the ten directions, and all coarse and fine realms appear distinctly in it without exception. Even matters of eighty thousand kalpas are not yet strange to it; how much more some hundreds, thousands, or ten million years? What you speak of — good and evil men, and the good and evil deeds they do — this is precisely where cause and effect are manifest and easily believed. But a hundred or a thousand years hence, though the evil man has not yet been born, his evil karma has already been fashioned many lives before, and the requital of enemies and debtors has already been plainly fixed in former lives. Because the karmic cause is not yet ripe and the evil condition has not yet arrived, though that man is caught up in the upside-down turning of rebirth within the worlds of the ten directions and does not himself know it, yet the sage has long since illumined him within the great treasury of light. And when the evil condition ripens and enemies meet and the evil fruit is accomplished — the end of the evil fruit is exactly like the beginning of the evil cause. Without waiting to stir the mind or move a thought, he naturally knows it clearly: this is what is called seeing that far-off time as if it were today. Such is the sage's mind of true permanence.

Moreover, cause and effect never err, not by a hair's breadth. It is said: though a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the deeds one has done do not perish; when cause and condition meet, the fruit is reaped by oneself. This is a principle that must be so. Can you, sir, truly believe in it? Seen in this light, the unvirtuous man is not appointed by Heaven; he makes himself so.
To Yin, Army Adviser

Since I parted from you, two years have slipped by in a blur. I hear that you are now on campaign and still among the Li. The steaming heat has passed; I trust your honored person is well. These people are no cunning rats; they are Heaven's people. To kill beyond measure greatly wounds the harmony of things, and I know you would not count it high merit. Yesterday when Liu Qinghai, the company commander of the garrison, left, I already instructed him again and again: by no means count killing as merit. When we meet we should be thorough and warm about it. I have an old clumsy piece, In Prospect of Qionghai, which says that the Li are a people of the highest antiquity. I write it on the head of a fan to make the meaning plain.
Reply to Zheng, Provincial Graduate

I have just received your letter, and so learn that you have quietly given your mind to this Way. You say that in the midst of daily use thoughts of good arise before you. Our nature is in itself originally good, but because it is dyed by the habits of the dusts, its spiritual brightness is obscured; thus in daily use men employ only the habits of feeling and not the truth of the nature. This is why common folk use it daily and do not know it; if they knew it, worthies and sages could be awaited at once. Just where, in daily use, a good thought arises before you and you do not forget it, that is the moment when your original face appears. If it appears before you at all times and you are aware of it in thought after thought, and your awareness reaches the ground of pure goodness, then the truth of the nature will of itself be restored, and the radiance of the original substance will of itself be disclosed.
Reply to Zou Nangao, Supervising Secretary

I have long dwelt where all ties are cut off; and lately phantom illness has come upon me again, so I am nursing my sickness in deep retreat and my ties are fewer still. Truly this is Heaven's gift to me of a man of leisure. Looking back at the dusty world, where men toil and fret all their lives, how many are there who can attain to being a man of no affairs? I think one who knows me must clap his hands over this from time to time. Relying on this protection of the Dharma, I have been able to rest in Chan and be still in the Laṅkāvatāra samādhi, and what I have entered grows deeper. Not long ago Wang Guanglu, together with Ding the Assistant Commissioner, went to keep an appointment with the governor at Duanzhou, and wrote to me that there is much rumor in the governor's office and many who slander this mountain rustic. The two of them argued for me with all their might, almost to the point of hair standing on end and eyes splitting. What is this, after all? From this I know that this Saha world of turbid soil, with its earth, stones, and mountains, cannot be spoken of in the same breath as the Pure Land whose ground is level as the palm of a hand.

Of the disciples who followed me north, because there was no gate at which to beg, I have now sent them all home. Only this mountain rustic dwells alone, lodging here as a traveler, which is all the lighter and freer. Withered trees and cold cliffs are no less than in former days; without this there is no way to break the steaming heat or disperse the poison of miasma. The times are such that the affairs of state are hard and the common people strain their necks to see; let the greatly compassionate one ferry them across. I pray you take effort to eat well, hold yourself dear for the sake of the realm, and love yourself for the sake of the Way.

Time and again I have received your letters, and your compassionate thoughts have been earnest and thorough beyond measure. None but one of the same substance in great compassion, who loves all things with an equal mind, could be so deeply concerned. In this hardship of mine I have been fortunate to be able to consult the good teachers within the dust, and have held myself with care; what I have entered of the Dharma gate is not shallow. In recent years, in solitude, pain, and emptiness, I am no less than in deep mountains and remote valleys: all conditions shut out, my traces never entering the world. Of those who know me in the city, only Wang Xuncheng is one; in a whole year I do not cross his threshold three times. Fortunately I am able to keep company with Youwu from time to time; he is truly bone and flesh at the edge of the sky, never forgotten at a single meal. Not only does he aid me in the Way and in righteousness, but even the supplies he provides come out of his own mouth's portion. Our lives lean on each other; this stretch of karma is by no means shallow. This gentleman's liver and gallbladder shine on men like the mirror of Qin; meeting things and responding to occasions, he penetrates to the five inward organs. As a bearer of the Way, he may be called a vessel of the highest faculties. Through this forging by heavenly virtue, his progress is far from ordinary, and another day he will adorn buddha-lands and bring living beings to maturity beyond conception. When we meet he must be joyful beyond measure.

In Guangdong, since the year gengzi, the face of the world has changed; each day grows more perilous and crooked, and the waves of the sea of suffering stretch without horizon. I drift with the wind, finding no rest at all. Only now do I know that for the ancients to be master within the dust was no small matter, and that to be liberated according to conditions is truly hard to attain. I often recall the words you urged upon me at parting, and when I received your letters, earnestly pressing the same point over and over. As the proverb has it: would you know the road down the mountain? Ask one who has come and gone. Unless you had deeply entered the samādhi of the illusory, how could you penetrate the Dharma like this?

I have heard that the blazing flames of affliction are precisely the furnace of worthies and sages, and that the various habits of attachment cannot be melted away without them. Had it not been for the sacred grace, how could I have come to this? The longer it goes, the more I see that this grace is great and hard to repay. To turn toil in the dust into the Buddha's work here, and further to make boundless merit for the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi — this comes from a true and earnest bitter heart, and compared with those who in former days rested beneath the tree of no sorrow and ate the rice of the great household, it is as heaven to earth.

The fountainhead of the ancestral Way at Caoxi was choked with filth and had long been a demon's den; now it has been swept clean. There are still koans unfinished, and my strength here is spent. I was just about to send to your reverence to ask you to be a vajra banner, when your messenger arrived. Is this not the Patriarch's intent receiving and gathering us? I respectfully take the circumstances here and set out their general shape, to be held up to your wisdom-light. If you think of the Dharma's decline and this Way's desolation, I pray you let the sound of the heavenly drum resound and proclaim it to all who have affinity, that they may awaken in a single dream. What do you say?

Anxiety and hardship, and human feeling — all are the original substance. Without grasping the tally of the utmost real, how could one turn affliction into bodhi and birth-and-death into nirvāṇa? In recent years you, sir, have dwelt in circumstances such as these; one may know that you have turned greatly indeed. Without this, how would you while away the time? From of old, students of the Way have passed over the crucial juncture of life and death with a swing of the arm; the ancients could not know them all. In recent years, Luo Jinxi is such a man. My body is in the land of miasma while my mind stays at your side; there is no time when we are not together. Therefore all your various samādhis are perfectly clear and hidden from me in nothing.

In Lingnan, since Caoxi's teaching waned, Dadian's echo has died away and the Jiangmen school has not risen; then came Elder Yang Fu, who raised on high the banner of the nature school. I am fortunate to sit in that place, and my joy and praise never end. The students, by worldly habit, have somewhat broken their attachments; this too is a foundation for opening and transforming. Yesterday Elder Fu wrote a preface to the Caoxi Record, truly every piece of it a red heart; one might say his tongue drags on the ground. I present it to you; be pleased to read it, and be glad for these many deluded ones.
To Yue Shifan

Since we parted I have twice received your letters, and so know of the clamor among the Zou and Lu. Alas! When the straight way is no longer tolerated at court, and one is cast off by his own countryside as well, the state of the world may be known. I hear you have taken refuge in the provincial capital, which is no long-term plan. I have heard that a bodhisattva tames and subdues living beings by entering deeply into the samādhi of the illusory; this is originally no real dharma, and you have long entered this gate. I hope you will not brood over it deeply; there will be those who reconcile matters, and a laugh may well dissolve it all. I have divined a hidden dwelling on Mount Kuang, and it suits me well. But as for the protector of the Dharma you speak of, he has the heart to shoulder the burden, yet the gate of giving is not yet opened and nothing has been accomplished. If Mañjuśrī would stretch out his right hand from afar, then the tower gate would open at once. Can you be without such a thought?

Formerly you did me the honor of visiting me in the prison of Sicheng, no less than Ānanda inquiring after Devadatta in the Iron Enclosure. At that time ghee was poured into my mouth and sweet dew sprinkled on my heart, and it made a strange event between the two realms. Counting on my fingers over this dusty world, how could such a thing be seen again? Lately, in the assembly, I beheld the vajra flames flashing in men's eyes; since we parted I could not in the end hold back a smile, and I spoke out early. I wonder whether, in the sea of cessation, bubbles still now and then arise and burst. I have walked into the land of miasma, and I rely on the Buddha and Patriarchs' spiritual power to gather and uphold me: I take the cart's dust as a jeweled seat and the horsewhip as a whisk, and from time to time I go among the realms of rākṣasas to talk of the unborn. I cause countless skulls to open their eyes and light to break the darkness. Truly I do not know whether I am driven by the power of karma, or whether it is brought about by the power of vows. One who knows me, hearing of it, will surely grant me a spit.
To Yu Deyuan, Ministry Official

From afar I gaze toward you, sir, seated on the lion of Tianmu, shouting at the white ox in the open ground, at play among the three monasteries of West Lake, where water is enough and grass is enough. And more: you take Maitreya as your teacher and Vasubandhu as your younger brother, listen to the precepts of the nature, and behold the flower of light. Of the joy of that cessation, I know the long broad tongue cannot proclaim a single ten-thousandth.

As for me, I invited an empty fruit with an empty flower, and carried a heap of guilt into a land of guilt. Though the Dharma-nature suffers no loss, yet as for the deluded in their thoughts, they cannot but hold an upside-down view. If one such as you looks at me with the Dharma eye, how much can he see? When Jueyin came, he brought your excellent words, a full foot in thickness; deeply do I receive the utmost of your compassionate thoughts. To see the refinement of your protection of the Dharma truly makes a man's pores ache and sting. Alas, in this age of the Dharma's decline, the buddha-nature in us is like a divine pearl in a privy: not only does its light not show, but the stench drives men off. And this is far from being merely a night-blooming flower or a pretty face.
To Fan Youxuan, Censor

I have received your letters, one after another, filling several volumes, and so know all your comings and goings. When Master Ke came, I learned further that you are well, peaceful, and happy. The samādhi in this is like a man drinking water: he alone knows the cold and warmth. Master Ke has been parted from me for a year, and he too has improved so much. This is enough to show that anxiety, hardship, and adversity are all aids to the equipment of the Way. For you to have found so good a friend in the land of miasma is surely a matter of heavenly affinity.

The karmic occasion of the new Laṅkāvatāra commentary all arose from the mind without marks, transforming into merit. Now, relying on your added blessing, it has been roughly completed. I first send you one copy to ask for correction; I trust that as you let your eyes wander in quiet, you will find places where something has leaked out. I beg you ten thousand times to point them out with your golden lancet, and so make yet another great gift of Dharma. I hear that the students at your gate advance daily. I have heard that the Tathāgata does not forsake a single living being, and takes great compassion as foremost. The land of miasma is precisely the ground of your vow of compassion; I hope you will not weary of ferrying them across. This is the good fortune of the Way.
To Xing Meiyang, Provincial Graduate

Jiangzhou is the place of the near-by monasteries and benefactors of the patriarchs of Mount Kuang, and the seeds of prajñā are especially many here. But those who scorch them are also many; you alone put forth sprouts and send out shoots, spread blossoms and ripen fruit, standing out beyond those who came before. Had your vow not been deep, you could not have held your roots fast like this. Master Da comes and goes among the layered clouds and the Five Elders; without you to wander with him, how would the mountain spirit take on color? I have admired you long, and regret only that I have no chance to take your arm.
To Qu Dongguan

My two friends Zhongfu and Wenqing have gone to the capital; Master Miao has already arrived. In the swim of Dharma joy you will surely not be lonely. I reflect that in this age of the Dharma's decline there is no one for the two truths; only you manifest the body of a magistrate and preside over this Way. One may say your gift of Dharma is without end. I pray you use your boundless great compassion to save those not yet saved, so that seeing and hearing they may gain benefit, planting the seed of wisdom in this life and realizing bodhi in lives to come. At that time, looking back at former causes, they may well find that it began today.

The gentlemen I met before are all men of genuine and keen faith; I pray you will from time to time water the seedlings of the spirit with the water of Dharma, and not fail the seeds they planted long ago. For this you must use the samādhi of the illusory net to enter all their bodies, and with all-wisdom skillfully turn and adapt. Who but you could do it? I know well that I am broken and rent, and that I bring the robe into disrepute; yet I dare not add to my arrogance. My good fortune is that I am held in your hearts, and I truly look for the non-dual. What joy can I express? Since my return all thoughts are ashes, and my single mind has nowhere to rest; day by day I sink into withered stillness. Those few words at parting were truly for myself. The times are such that the burning house is ablaze and the five heats are burning; I pray you restrain yourself for the sake of the Way and do not weary of ferrying and helping. This is my utmost hope.

You have looked upon me with compassionate eyes and presented me with the Comprehensive Lamp of the Five Houses; this is your gift to me of samādhi. I, a mountain monk, consult it constantly, deeply ashamed that my faculties are dull and inferior and that I cannot see the ancients face to face. Yet I have roughly grasped the matter of cutting away the edge of views. I regret only that I have not yet given that one great shout of awakening, to make it the joy of my life. From now on I shall take up the topic of inquiry; another day I may perhaps have something to repay one who knows me. How would I dare forget the ground of the cause?

Only you, sir, press your finger on every mote of dust, and the ocean-seal gives forth light; whatever thing you meet you raise and proclaim, and all is the Buddha's work. But I wonder whether among those newly resolved there are any able to bear the great matter. I pray you do not turn from your original vow, but tame and subdue them according to what fits, and cause them to plant vajra seeds. I often think of the remnant granted by Bhīṣmagarjita and the dust left by Jñānottara: if one should chance upon the assembly at Vulture Peak, one would think they were not of this kind — but then who would be the fitting vessel when the Tathāgata comes into the world? And those who come after will look on us as we look on them. What does your reverence think?

You have come to see Many Treasures and inquired after the World-Honored One: are there no longer many beings of pride and jealousy? This I should ask of you. I pray you constantly cherish and protect yourself for the sake of the Way.

Since we parted at the Dragon Flower, it is now only today that I look back at the world and see it truly as a dream. To think of meeting and speaking heart to heart as at our first gathering — how could that come again? Only your vow to benefit living beings grows daily wider and your gate of entering principle daily deeper; blessing and wisdom both complete, in the practice that benefits self and others alike, you go straight on into the vajra mind-ground.

I am blown and drummed by the wind of karma, and have come to this. Yet I am glad that the samādhi of the illusory plucks me from the pit of the obstacle of principle; this I owe to the spiritual power of the Buddhas, who make a bridge for me. I think that you who know me must greatly rejoice for me. In the winter of bingshen I was exiled; when I set out south I took leave of you, layman Tianchi, at the capital gate, and had meant to go by way of Huanggang and enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti. Unexpectedly the road went otherwise, and I passed Nankang; since entering the land of miasma I have relied on your compassionate covering, and have been quite able to drink the air of miasma with an ice-and-snow heart and intestines. In another three years I may escape injury to the four elements.

I once remember talking with you by night on the tenets of the three teachings, and using consciousness-only to verify the purport of the two masters. You graciously sealed my mind with yours. At that time I was returning to the seaside, and I happened to write it down as a book, called On the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi. Only now has it been cut in wood. Junior Minister Yang called it a settled judgment for a thousand ages. As for the Laṅkāvatāra, I have often lamented that reading it one cannot punctuate the sentences. The First Patriarch pointed to it as the mind-seal, yet the schools of Chan and of doctrine have become sworn enemies over it. Lately, by the sacred grace, I have been granted a place of leisure; deeply grieving that I have no way to atone for the fault of ruining the Dharma, I have in the leisure from bearing arms applied my strength to this sūtra. Whenever a single phrase brought gain, I wrote it down at once; unwittingly I came to the end of the scroll. I respectfully send it together with the former treatise, and ask that your Dharma eye decide and choose. If it is not mistaken, then I shall not only have made this journey to no purpose; I shall truly have lived this life to no purpose. Yet this is only the dregs of words and letters, not enough to bring forth the source of the nature in the man himself. As for setting up gateposts for the Buddha and Patriarchs and singing obliquely and communicating sideways, it may serve to draw out a single thread.
The Dream Wanderings of Elder Hanshan, Volume Seventeen
To Wang Jingfeng, Minister of War

I remember how on the great road of Chang'an we walked arm in arm, driving our lean donkeys far ahead, eating in the wind and lodging on the road. This stretch of karma was truly a strange thing between the two realms. Since then, in the blink of an eye, all has melted away like this. Seen with the true eye, it is simply an empty flower, a dream. Only the spiritual power of samādhi enters deeply into the reality of all dharmas as dream and illusion.

Since I entered the land of miasma I have relied on your light shed upon me, and all conditions are still. Every kind of thing has become an aid to the equipment of the Way, and I feel the more the sacred grace, which has torn apart the layered nets of illusion; this may surpass half a lifetime of pilgrimage. I know that one who knows me will not take this for wild talk. Ma Zu proclaimed the Way in Jiangxi, and the monasteries of Mount Lu are all places where the family tradition of the ancestors unfolded. You were born in Huangmei and opened your teaching at Qingyuan, and now you are again master of Mount Kuang. This sort of pilgrimage all comes from the time when Ma Zu loosened the precepts; can you not weigh this original vow again? I hear that Guizong has lately received the sacred grace of a great bestowal. The causes and conditions of today are far from what they were; and with you as its lord, the people too are not what they were. The revival of the Dharma of Jiangxi is to be hoped for from you. I pray you take the vajra mind-ground as your protection of the Dharma and your giving across; I stand waiting to see the endless wheel of Dharma turn within a single mote of dust.

That which bodhi takes as its condition is the condition of suffering beings. You, sir, by the power of your vow of great compassion, place yourself in the realm of suffering beings; so even in your dreams there is nothing but the work of benefiting living beings. I know that the seed of bodhi grows day and night, and must be beyond measure. The bodhisattva of the fifth ground in the Avataṃsaka works purely for others and thereby perfects his own wondrous practice; how could one who solidifies his notion of self and clings to a solitary liberation ever compare?

Thus the thousand peaks of Ziyun are never absent from your mat. At the river's head we met to part, and the words you earnestly pressed upon the chief seat as I set out on my journey entered one by one into my deepest samādhi. For more than twenty years I have sunk in the sea of suffering, and waking or sleeping I think of the mountains and forests as of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. What good fortune that, relying on the gathering power of your compassion, I am placed on the summit of a ten-thousand-fathom peak; a single night's peace there is doubled day upon kalpa. Having come to this place where the water ends and the mountains cease, how could I allow the least deluded thought to settle? This is my own proper business, and I dare not trouble you with many instructions.

I look up to receive your gifts of giving, as protection for the mountains and forests. The few rafters at Wuru were already settled last winter, and I keep my peaceful dwelling. What did I ever expect of my remaining years, that I should attain to lying high at ease? Ten thousand mountains piled with snow, a single path sealed in cloud — it is no less than the bone-piercing cold of the cliffs of Qingliang. Grateful thoughts for your heart of protecting the Dharma truly cannot be expressed in thanks.

Since I first heard the alarm, my mind has galloped to the frontier every day without fail. In this small kalpa I regret that I have no spiritual power to dissolve the fixed karma of living beings; I can only lead the assembly to recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra daily, praying for peace on the borders. I earnestly wish that you, elder layman, may soon fulfill your resolve to return, and that together we may bring to completion the vow of the Pure Land in this life.

With the new year I hear that your carriage has already reached home; I was so glad I could not sleep. This I owe to the sacred grace, beyond all hope. Truly it is the added power of the Buddha and Patriarchs, and may serve as testimony to the faith of the Dharma gate. Is it a small matter? I often think that you have sat through these two years and quietly observed a single thought; it is nothing less than an iron wall and a silver mountain, and even thirty years of pilgrimage might not yield such a place of true strength. Having passed this one barrier, you will swing your arm toward the Pure Land, and surpass a day and a kalpa besides. So I know that all this karma of yours is a swift sail to carry you out of the sea of birth and death. What joy is like it?

I rely on your compassionate shelter. My mountain dwelling is not yet three years old, but my management has made it just habitable. I have now handed the permanent residence over to the chief seat for the community of the ten directions; only this single body of mine remains, in closed retreat and cut off from ties, eating gruel and rice with the assembly. From mid-autumn until now five months have passed. A condition sought in vain for thirty years is fulfilled at once; how could I bear to let my remaining years slip lightly away? I shall set aside all Chan talk and Buddha-Dharma and practice only the clumsy method: following Huiyuan's six periods, I shall mark incense sticks in place of the water clock, and recite Amitābha's name fifty thousand times a day to see out my remaining years. Fortunately my decayed and withered body still has the strength to press on; I sit at night without lying down, and my spirit feels no weariness. Every single day is your gift to me, elder layman.
To Miao Juexiu

You and I have been companions in the Dharma through many lives, and have been parted and scattered at the crossroads. Now, in a strange land, to go straight on as we do — what joy and comfort is this? The Dharma affinities along the West River have depended on the wisdom of the one who first made them clear; and even my casual passing through relies deeply on your sideways communication to bring them to light. Here is the king's weighty gift and the Buddha's cherished inner secret, and the occasion that answers is one that meets by chance: its wonder lies in the beats coming together to make the music.

I privately think that wherever there are Dharma affinities, if each person would tap and peck at the same moment, then men like you would cause the light of the Dharma banner to illumine the whole earth. After we parted, all that has happened is fully set out in Nangao's letter. But I think of you going down east in your little boat to see old friends, and you cannot be without longing; and I do not know where Master Da's staff has come to rest, or whether you can once draw near and bow at his feet. I bear the burden of my heap of guilt and cannot draw near to a lone cloud. If you would raise your staff and shoes and come with the autumn mood, that is indeed my great wish; but the journey is hard and toilsome, and I fear you could not bear the fatigue. If there is affinity for us to sit together at the head of the Wuyang River and peel away the ten thousand things together, that too would be a strange event.

By the power of former karma and following the conditions of illusion, I have unworthily taken on the robe, a guest not matching the reality, bringing some slight blemish on the pure truth. Lately the Buddhas in their compassion have not cast me off, but have thrown me into the blazing flames of the red furnace, suddenly burning away all the accumulated habits and tangled defilements until they are well-nigh gone. I rejoice that this stretch of karma may surpass a lifetime of pilgrimage.

Recently, lingering among the walled barracks of the provincial capital, I sit withered behind a closed door all day, searching out the mind-seal of the Buddha and Patriarchs and finishing koans not yet finished. In this age of the Dharma's decline, with the waves of the sea of suffering, I seek only to save myself; how dare I hope to turn the helm in midstream and set sail for the other shore? Therefore my fly-whisk is heaped with dust and my mouth corners grow moldy. Lately I have been fortunate to have Yunyuan coming and going morning and evening, which may be called a rare encounter outside the world. This gentleman has a natural bone of the Way; whatever he says and does flows from the reality of the vajra mind. Though the Way is not yet a match for his habits, I am glad that his habits do not obstruct the Way — all the more extraordinary. This is because prajñā has long perfumed him and his root is free of glue, with no stickiness at all. Among the items of the Way he may be called a bold and powerful true man, a vessel of the highest faculties; a single prod and he turns, and he may double a day into a kalpa.

This forging by the maker of things has brought no small accomplishment. Observe how he treats honor and disgrace as chaff, and life and death as dust; how he accords with things with an empty heart and winds through the turbid world — very different from former days. I intend that on the day you and I meet again, we may perhaps no longer treat him as a younger brother. When you went east to Wu, I reckon that by now you have turned your boat back to Nanzhou. If you have news of Master Da's daily life, and of our old friends, I pray you tell me, to comfort me. How does Erzhan fare? I hear that Yunju has been restored and the ancestral Way in Jiangzuo is reviving; the turning of the Dharma-wheel's axle lies in this one turn. Now that you, sir, bear it with strength, is it not that in a former life you were the steward, and have now come to finish this old vow? As for Youwu's going or staying, he will report it himself; let that set your mind at rest. But my phantom shadow and drifting traces still depend on the shield of walls, and I have not yet ascended the first ground.
To He Zhiren, Grand Secretary

Since I crossed the mountain pass, all has been as distant as another world; how could the kinship of the Way be forgotten for a single day? Since the winter of guimao, when I heard the news of Master Da's death, this heart of mine has died with him. The Dharma banner is broken; where shall those with understanding turn? It is not only a matter of a grieving heart. I earnestly ponder the meaning of Master Da's death: I had hoped, on the day I gained release, to go in person and offer a single petal of incense. Afterwards I met with ever more hardship, never resting my feet, until in the winter of guichou I left Guangdong, intending to pass by Mount Nan and keep my appointment with an old friend, and so take the eastern road home. How could I have expected that in the blink of an eye three more years would pass? How much is a human life? And now I am past seventy, and the prospect before me is not long. I have just heard that his relics have already entered the stupa, which adds to my fear and trembling: I dread that I may at once fill a ditch or gully, and with what face shall I see Master Da in the stillness and light?

Now I shall go down east in a little boat, and by autumn or winter I may reach Shuangjing, to keep the pact of life and death. In his lifetime he promised me the stupa inscription; how can this vow be broken again? But of Master Da's pilgrimage before his middle years I know nothing at all; I must inquire and discuss with the eminent disciples of the various gates so that I may take up the brush. Master Da's seamless stupa must first be produced from the tips of your several brushes; I do not mind being the one who draws the gourd after the pattern.
To Yu Zhongfu, Ministry Official

One meeting must serve for a thousand days; it is as a single meal's time. Though the light of the mind illumines all, it is still not so good as to clear the throat and cough together now and then. Master Da has gone west on a journey without asking leave, which makes a man's deluded thoughts grow again.

Last autumn, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I made a phantom journey to the royal city, and was fortunate to meet laymen Dongguan, Jianzhai, and the rest, and to exhaust the delight of Dharma joy. Only at the side of the lotus seat was there one man sitting cross-legged too few; that was the one omission from the ceremony. I imagine that when you enter the capital, the Dharma gate takes on color. But in the dust-heaps of Chang'an, every mote of dust is a place for entering right concentration; can you enter them one by one? As for what you say — a single firm and dense body appears in every mote of dust — I fear only that it is not firm and dense. My foolishness grows daily as the years come on, and my laziness increases; I lie about listlessly with nothing to do. I think that seen from your samādhi, it must call up a serene smile. When shall I briefly have leisure to sit with you in silence and talk of the non-dual? The land and sea have no shore; may the boat of wisdom ever lie across, and may you not weary of ferrying others. This is my wish.

Formerly, in the space of a single brushing of arms, I already dared to take it upon myself to say that I knew you; but I did not dare to say that you knew me. Having read your letter, I see your true heart plainly, the two shining on each other like the mirrors of Qin exchanging light, so that liver and gallbladder are wholly exposed. Not only do I see the craftsman's wondrous work; I also see deeply your natural true color, with no trace of the axe at all. Compared with one whose wood cannot be sawn apart and whose grain runs crosswise in knots, though one had an adze that could slice off the tip of a nose, there would be no place to apply its skill.

I reflect only that as the age declines and the Way grows faint, all flows lower and lower. It is not only that men who take life and death as urgent business and the Dharma as their own charge, standing out towering like the ancients, are not to be found; even those of true faith who understand black and white and who with a straight heart and warm entrails throw their bodies across the ruts of the road are rarely seen. How much less one who stands out towering and at once transcends the turbid world, as you and the great assembly of fellow practitioners do, all pressing forward at once. I privately hold that though the age be one of the Dharma's decline, it is still the true Dharma. Since then we have had those lofty, deep, firm, and sharp, on whom we rely as outer protection; and though we do not go at it head-on with fierceness, it is enough to make demons and outsiders lose their souls. This great city of nirvāṇa of ours can be kept in peace while we sit. How much more when the work is renewed daily and there is one who personally superintends the labor? The good fortune of our Way — to what shall I liken it?

I have often privately argued: our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world for the sake of one great matter. But what matter is this one great matter? The ancients said: set aside birth and death, the one truly great matter; all the rest may be discussed. Hence one knows that only he who truly sees birth and death, is perfectly clear and unmoved, and does not flinch from it, may be called fit to bear the great matter. And if one can indeed understand that birth and death do not change, then all the rest need not be discussed. If one takes this matter as great, then all else is a trifle. Thus there must be a difference between one who forgets his life for the Dharma and one who wounds his life for the desires of things.

But if one employs Tian Dan and Cheng Ying's hearts in the service of the Dharma, the Dharma will have nothing that is not roused; and if one applies Su Wu and Li Ling's resolve to subduing demons, no demon will fail to submit. Then the work of bringing peace to the land of Dharma is greater than anything. This is what you deeply embrace, and what the great assembly of fellow practitioners share; I seem to know it deeply. Therefore the task of shouldering it cannot but be entrusted to you, and I would have you take it upon yourself. Though we are grand and imposing, we are only mud and wooden buddhas: are we not towering and fine to look at? We are fit to receive incense and scattered flowers as offerings, but we cannot save anyone from water or fire.

When the attendant returns, he will speak with all his heart of how wondrously you have matched the meaning beyond words, and how you have graciously given your heart to me. Thus whoever stands guard and defends the Dharma banner — you will surely illumine what has not yet come with your Dharma eye and hold it with your spiritual power. I now specially send to welcome Master Longhua back to the cave, and I keep Master Da to preside over the place of stillness. The holding back and letting go of these two elders lies in your hands too. Ha, ha — one laugh, and a thousand li share the same sound. All this I submit to your compassionate regard.

I was blown south by the wind of karma; at first I meant to pass by the old capital and see old friends, but unexpectedly I went west upriver and so lost the good meeting. Fortunately at the river's head I struck palms with Master Da, and we parted after two nights. Counting on my fingers, in the blink of an eye it is nearly four years. The face of the world flows on and does not abide even for an instant; only with the eye of the Way does one see that there is no thought of coming or going.

When I first arrived in Leiyang, this body of outflows seemed not to mix with the water and fire there; but by melting it with the nature, all is equal and still. When I returned to Wuyang, I gained Youwu as a companion, and we were together morning and evening without break. This gentleman's seed of light is very deep, but he is obscured by habit-energy; time and again I pricked him with the needle and could not penetrate, until at the very moment of parting I laid on a poisonous hand and gave him one needle at the crown of the head. He said himself that it went in to the bottom, and only then did he know how to turn his head and turn his mind. So I gave him the name Layman Juefei, and wrote an inscription for it. He too made a great vow of himself: if after this he does not bitterly urge himself on, then he should not be counted among men. Those words came from a painful heart. But this matter requires that from time to time one decide and clarify it with a good teacher and be lifted along by him, and only then can one keep to the ruts. Otherwise, as soon as evil habits arise, one falls unawares into the black mountain and the ghost cave. This has always been the difficulty for students of the Way: the point is to set one's feet firm on the vajra mind-ground, and then one will not be tossed about by it.

Lately I have received your letter, and so know how you have met with anxiety and hardship in recent years, such as a man can hardly bear. Had you not used principle to bend feeling, how could you have passed this one barrier? The waves within it are the vast ocean of the nature-sea; I reckon that bathing in the flood and wandering in the great deep, your boundless measure can of itself drink up the hundred rivers and swallow the sun and moon. I showed your letter to Youwu, and when he read to the earnest words, he found his tongue too short and, because the true spirit pressed on him, could only nod. Even in all the universe, one who pours himself out in such substantial work is rarely seen.

The Laṅkāvatāra is now finished; I specially send an attendant to carry it to you and ask your correction. But the realm of this sūtra cannot be reached by climbing after conditions. You, in the midst of mourning, where principle is exhausted and feeling forgotten, must be entering deeply into this gate. If a single phrase accords with your mind, I pray you tell it to those of like mind and widen its gift of Dharma. In this I do not merely repay the sovereign's grace in my small way; you too may thereby requite the boundless.

Since we parted, how the time has flown; so many years and months, and I do not know where they have fallen. Are the dreams of the world even come to this? In the land of miasma, steaming heat and poisonous fog are hard to endure when one meets them. What I rely on is a single spot of cool ground, to be my herb of invisibility. Fiery wilderness and northern snow, fire and water of different power — so it has been from of old. Yet last winter the cold here was no less than north of Ji, and in the new year I went south, lodging at a travelers' inn in Xinxing, where the cold pierced to the bone and I could not sleep for freezing. At midnight came a knocking at the door that startled me up, and there was Dayi with letters from the ancients of the north: the first packet from Master Da, and your letter with it. Reading them, I felt as if ice and snow had fallen upon my bedside and every pore of my body was lucid, as when, in a thousand-fathom cold cliff, one wakes from sleep with a patched robe over one's head.

In the fourth month, on my way back from Leilian, the Dharma sound arrived again. I held it in my hand: every word overflowed with the light of the mind, bursting and scattering so as to dazzle. You, sir, sitting amid this anxiety, illness, and suffering, still wrote so fine a letter — one sees that the heart of the elder of the three carts is at no time absent from the burning house. How have your affairs been these years? How does your nephew get on? In this age of the Dharma's decline, the fire of the kalpa blazes; if one can find a patch of cool ground in it, that is a lotus in fire.

Since Youwu took leave of me at the Pearl River, one awl at the crown of his head has gone through to the soles of his feet; relying on this occasion, his keeping to the house these years, closing the door and declining guests, and practicing the discipline of patience, all depend on the power of this Dharma gate. Only, his habits are bold and fierce, and he cannot at once enter the subtle and dense. Liu Yizhe's faculties are close to the Way, sharp and quick; but his prajñā is not deep. Such rare spirit in the world is seldom seen. Whenever we met I spoke only of light matters before our eyes, and never once dared raise this matter. To know the meaning of buddha-nature, one should observe the season and the conditions; I reckon he will not fail your high regard.

The news of Master Da in Chang'an greatly comforts my heart. His former manner has been cut back by more than half. This is not only Master Da's blessing; it is also a great fortune for the Dharma gate. That in the age of the Dharma's decline there should be such a master craftsman, one may look back toward the age of the semblance Dharma. Only the monasteries are in decline and the young have thin blessings; who knows whether they can be transformed. Caoxi has fallen into the utmost ruin, and I have taken pains to set it in order; last autumn I entered the mountain and made some repairs, and it seems now to be presentable. This is what is called a water-moon monastery and a buddha-work of empty flowers — so it is wherever one touches. Why must one make a field of blessing without marks with a mind that dwells on something? This is what the protectors of the Dharma with their refined hearts are glad to hear; I have added a laugh with my tiresome words.
To Wu Benru, Ministry Official

Since I took leave of your radiant countenance, a whole twelve years have passed in a flash. Since we parted, the Dharma gate has daily declined and the good teachers have scattered like stars. Painfully I think how the Dharma banner is broken and the sun of wisdom has sunk in the west; to speak of it corrodes the heart. I think that one of the same substance as you must be grieved beyond bearing. Of old it was said that Jiyin, for the sake of the Dharma, had the hearts of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu; now in our Master we see it again.

I am common and mean, and ashamed that I have no duty to bear the Dharma, while I have the fault of having broken it. Yet in the vajra mind I do not know what repentance to make. Drifting and sinking in the sea of miasma, I do not dare to betray my original heart; my good fortune is that I can be at peace in all suffering, which is enough to comfort your compassionate thoughts. Formerly at Caoxi I served as the Sixth Patriarch's servant and menial, sweeping and sprinkling, as a way of purifying the mind-ground. Relying on the shelter of the Dharma, things are in some rough order. I think only that the bonds of karma are not yet loosed and my first resolve is not yet fulfilled, so I dare not rest my mind in the stillness of concentration. If it be as I wish, that I may grow old at rest and bury my bones here and so finish the great matter of birth and death, then truly only Heaven can nourish it and only your compassion can praise it. I wonder whether Mañjuśrī's right hand can reach out past this hundred cities.
To Zeng Jinjian, Ministry Official

The Nārāyaṇa Cave is an ancient buddha's place of the Way, the spot where Vairocana with his own mouth gave the prediction. Buried away at the edge of the sea, for a thousand years it has been turned upside down by mlecchas. At first I came here to avoid demons; little did I know I had blundered into the demon realm. Truly, when karma belongs to former conditions, there is no escaping it. At such a time there is no spiritual power and no Dharma power to be used; one can only cast aside body and mind and endure in accordance with conditions, not setting oneself up as an enemy of demonic foes. How would I dare boast of Chan concentration and liberation, or of harmonizing principle and phenomena without obstruction?

I have often thought of the Lotus Sūtra's entrustment: to benefit living beings in the final age, one must first rouse the power of great patience and the power of great diligence. Alas, the yellow-faced old one had deep fear of this time. Yet if I, a mountain monk, do not have the power of great patience and great diligence, how shall I pull down the demons' banners and raise the Dharma banner? You have shown me the meaning of bondage and release. Truly the Dharma-nature knows no this and that; I have often said that the worldly and the world-transcending differ only as the born and the unborn. Yet in daily use, the various karmic illusions and all that flows and turns are the causes of birth and death. If one is not turned by them and does not forget the objects, and there is something one can endure, that is called the patience of the born. If one does not see anything to endure and there is nothing enduring either, that is the patience of the unborn. If patience reaches the unborn, then there is nothing not endured. Mind and object thus, thus, is also cessation.

But what is called demonic karma is not only enmity. Whenever a man rouses his mind and moves a thought in a way that does not accord with liberation, that wounds the Dharma body and harasses the true nature, all of that belongs to the demons. If we who have the will to work at the task and to escape birth and death cannot endure this, how can we be called men of power? We are born and dwell within the realm of endurance. If this place is not broken through, there is nothing to break through. Therefore one should simply take the power of great patience and great diligence as the highest truth — no matter whether the conditions of the Way were fixed beforehand or not, whether one's strength is equal or not. Do you truly believe it? Meeting face to face is hard; unwittingly I have leaked out all of this.

Formerly your flying light graciously came to the Ocean Seal; truly it was a rare good affinity of the age, and it at once became a vajra seed that will not be worn away through kalpas, and in the end must break through the bone and come forth. This is the able business of a great man; were it not for a man of great strength like you, who would dare shoulder it and look it in the face? After we parted I had no way to learn the details; I trust that in your daily life you have already entered deeply into the samādhi of the illusory and are no longer dual in movement and stillness.

For a while I was toyed with by mountain ghosts, and with the obstructive conditions of former karma added, I brought on this severe censure. Though it stains the Dharma gate, I am glad that it has increased my strength in the Way. What is said — that when the great fire burns, this land is at peace — is no idle saying. The ancients always took painful matters as the aiding and increasing condition of the Way, and the place of true strength is precisely here. Hearing this, will you make of it a drum smeared with poison? Now I have borne arms for half a year, and it is just when the season is most disastrous, with pestilence rising on every side and the people and their goods withering away. Truly it is pitiable. Therefore my bodhi mind grows the more. But this illusory empty body is still very much in the burning house. The Dharma assembly at Vaiśālī, the talk of the non-dual — when shall it truly be? Only a compassion of one substance must surely make this withered old ascetic from time to time start up a deluded thought.
To Feng Qinan, Provincial Graduate

This old man has wandered with you for nearly twenty years, as in the light of moon on water; all adverse and favorable circumstances are but shadows within the light. You all entered together, yet your enjoyment differs, just as gods and men eat from one vessel and the fine and coarse are each distinct. This is why buddha-nature values the seed of conditions. This old man and you and the others met once in many lives, like a timely rain; each seed sprouted and ripened accordingly, and whether it bore fruit lay with the man.

Now that this old man is leaving Guangdong, it is like a season that has not yet come; fortunately you are there to water, so that it does not wither. This stretch of karma is truly no small thing. The two vehicles merely fear that living beings are hard to save, and so cut themselves off from bodhi. Would you keep living beings out of your sight? On the whole, this matter lies in a man's own consenting; where he consents is where he enters. The ancients cast away body and life, and it was only a consenting mind. I only wish that you would take consenting as your way with others, and then there will be none who do not consent. Think only that if this life is missed and this human body is lost, ten thousand kalpas will find it hard to regain; then there is no room for not consenting.

This old man knows in his heart that Dharma conditions are hard, and this journey was driven by the narrow habits of the mountains and forests. When the mad mind suddenly rested, I looked at the spirit of Mount Nan, which the patriarchs raised up, and now it is exhausted; its vital force is in difficulty. Now I lodge east of the lake, as Master Sheng once dwelt at Tiger Hill. Shansun is returning from the north and will soon enter Guangdong with Chunch'an; you may learn all from him. I know you are prone to illness; this is a Dharma gate you know by heart. I pray that in your room there may never be lacking a lion seat, so that all who come may together enter the samādhi of illusory illness, and then this illness will be a banner of diligence.
To Long Yuanwen

When this old man first came to Guangdong, you were the first to enter the Dharma gate and became the elder of the laymen; in twenty years of wandering together we have never dwelt in sound, voice, form, or appearance. Now that this old man leaves Guangdong, I rely on you to stand as the elder of the Dharma gate.
