Your refined heart in protecting the Dharma is like a vajra banner; only take to heart the protecting, remembering, and entrusting, and by all manner of skillful means draw in and gather those with affinity, so that the life of wisdom is not cut off. Let this be the highest truth. The wonder lies in the pointing that is beyond words: you have your own nostril that lifts to the sky, so how could it be pierced by one stalk of this old man's eyebrow?

Formerly the World-Honored One would not allow Ānanda to hear the Dharma with the conditioned mind, and the Chan gate does not allow language to turn the correct. The point is to bring out the man's own way of doing things. Why bind men with real dharmas? This old man is moved by your diligence for the Dharma and your earnest bitter heart, and how could he bear to forget the feeling? I wish only that this Way not fall, and then a thousand years will be as one day. What then of coming and going? The spirit of Mount Nan is exhausted; all the places of the Way have been left to the wild thickets, which cuts the heart. I fear that even if the elders rose again, it would not be easy to raise them up. Alas, the Way and the times — how can one force them?
To Yuanwen and Qinan

You think of how this old man has dealt with you all these eighteen years, very much like a magician performing his illusions at a crossroads. Though there were all manner of fair and foul, glad and sorrowful appearances, in the end they all come back to the magician. Looked at today, they are a dream as well. This old man's first thought was to take Mount Nan as a place of great rest; but when he arrived, he learned that the mountain is not fit for growing old in, and that every kind of thing is difficult, all of it a burden to body and mind. And being decayed and worn, I have no equipment for the victory of pilgrimage; I can only let go according to conditions and make do east of the lake. Fortunately one or two benefactors helped me build a retreat. Last winter I cut thatch and built a hut, and by the last day of the year I was already settled. At once the mad mind suddenly rested, and what I had wished for all my life was gained in a single morning. The bitterness and hardship of twenty years have melted into a realm of unsurpassed wondrous joy. Truly purity and defilement follow the mind, and suffering and joy lie with oneself: there is no place that is not the true realm of still light.

Most joyful of all, I have received the vast grace of the sovereign and have been given back my original face, and I covet nothing else. As for receiving visitors at the monastery gate, I rely on Master Zhan to bear that. From now on this old man will close his door, eat his fill, and sleep high; all Chan talk and Buddha-Dharma I tie up and put on a high shelf. Today I am at last a man of no affairs between heaven and earth. The peace of this one day surpasses a whole lifetime of bustle. Hearing it, will you not greatly rejoice for me?

Master Xiu lives with me, and from time to time he rouses this matter; I regret only that I cannot share it with you all. The ancients said that the roads differ but the care of the household is the same. If you can truly take this old man's joy as your own joy in every place and in daily use, then what this old man has, you also have; and what this old man lacks, you also lack. What is called one body, one wisdom, the power of wisdom and fearlessness — it is the same. Was this saying the yellow-faced old one's own? Do not say that this old man's affair today is utterly cut off from you all. Just where in daily use your deluded thoughts cross and your afflictions knot together — that is precisely this old man's present moment. If you miss it face to face, then you are separated by the mountains of Yue and the waters of Chu.

This year is precisely the time when your vow-power ripens. I remember how in Mañjuśrī's cave there were ten thousand followers, and yet several dozen seats stood empty; and each man has a patch of cloud beneath his feet — how could he be willing to let another ride it? But if there is one weary of fording and bridging, then Qinan, the chief seat, should strike the gavel for the assembly.
Reply to Li Xiangzhou, Court Historian

From the moment I entered the gate of emptiness I cherished a resolve directed upward. At nineteen I put on the black robe and thereupon cast aside brush and inkstone, and single-mindedly investigated the matter beneath my own feet. Ten years slipped by without my attaining awakening. So I hid my traces in the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, tormenting body and mind, until I reached a place where I could not recognize even a single word; and suddenly the four elements fell away and I had nothing to lean on. Looking back at the mountains and rivers and the world of former days, all were matters of a dream. Thereby I gained great happiness; and meeting every condition, I was like an image in a mirror, utterly without obstruction. So it was for eight years.

Before that I had not really understood the sūtras. Then I thought of the Buddha's Śūraṅgama Sūtra, which takes the three contemplations of the one mind as its tenet. Formerly I had been obstructed by words and letters; so I stilled my mind and contemplated carefully, taking contemplation of principle as the main thing. Once the contemplation of principle is penetrated, the rest of the text may be passed over. Afterwards I hid myself in the Eastern Sea and applied my strength to investigate deeply, and suddenly there was a gain. So I set it out directly in this book, believing it myself must be true. But among the doubting in the Dharma gate there will be some. Having long admired your profound understanding, I specially ask for your seal and correction; there should be a place where we may decide face to face. Just now I am troubled by the mischief of the illness-demon. If there is a time in the clear autumn, I should shut the door with you for ten days and once settle the plain intent of my life, so that this Way, thin and few, may not be alone in the world. At daybreak I go upriver; looking back, I have only longing to lean on.
Sent to Gao Yingtai, Prefect

Lately the times alarm the heart. Your strong resolve stirs and stirs; reading your draft, I learn the details of your recent situation. Yet for a subject to pour out his loyalty for the realm is his proper business; only this is not the hour for it, and it seems to violate the precept of using or laying aside. Moreover, at a matter of declining years, dwelling in a place of stubborn poverty, and just when a strong man loses countenance — is this not a great burden to body and mind? One who understands, weighing the heavy and the light, must surely have a single way to judge and settle it.

I am close to eighty, and decline and illness come daily. My good fortune is that I hide my traces in empty mountains and merely prolong a single breath, waiting for death. This withered heart has nothing with which to address one who knows me. If you could lower your mind into solitude and enjoy the joy of pure practice, making of it a stretch of karma that transcends the world, that would be a great strange event. The ancients said: the heart has sorrows beyond number in a lifetime; if not in the gate of emptiness, where shall they be dissolved? This truly is what I hope for.
Reply to Tan Fuzhi

Lately I have taken a foot of ground east of the lake and built a hut on the shady side of the irrigation stream. Happily the work is done, and on the eighteenth of the month I entered the room and lay down at ease; dreams and imaginings are suddenly empty, and it is enough to amuse my old age. And I am glad to have a man of faith like you, with whom my spirit flows and communicates — one may say I am not lonely. When the traveler came I received the words in your letter; it seems you are working at the task on the level of views and knowledge. This comes of the depth of your faith and devotion.

Therefore the Śūraṅgama says: to establish knowing upon views and knowledge is the root of ignorance. This is what is called the gate of all calamities. It also says: views and knowledge without knowing — this is nirvāṇa. This is what is called the gate of all wonders. The views and knowledge spoken of here are by no means the realm of common feeling, deluded thought, and calculation; they are all brought forth from the work of the actual and the ground of true inquiry and true awakening. They are very far from being idle talk of the mouth to be taken as Buddha-Dharma.

Your faith is indeed firm, but you have not entered deeply into the Dharma, and so you at once produce all sorts of words about views and knowledge, all of which become idle talk. As for a good teacher, he will not make a favor of the Buddha-Dharma, nor will he give his seal of approval with a winter-melon stamp. What this old man said — that the views and knowledge of living beings are the Buddha's views and knowledge — was spoken by tracing back to before one was deluded. It is not that the deluded thoughts and views within delusion are to be taken as the Buddha's views and knowledge. If deluded thought were the Buddha's views and knowledge, then all living beings on earth would already be Buddhas, and what need would there be of practice? If ordinary deluded thought and feeling were taken as the realm of enjoyment, then everyone in the world who has not rid himself of lust and killing, of greed, anger, and self-indulgence, would be a Buddha. If you take it so, that is the speech of demons. How can one take a false view for true awakening?

The various things in your letter are none of them a place of true enjoyment. You need only cut away all your former views and knowledge, not leaving a hair; and at the place where not a single thought remains, when you vaguely glimpse a trace, only then may you speak of the matter within. If you take clever and nimble views and knowledge for correct understanding, it is exactly like taking donkey dung for a bright pearl. If you keep such views and knowledge under the gate of a good teacher, then the good teacher too becomes a species of demon. This old man feels great Dharma love for you, and so does not spare his eyebrows in answering your intent. Try examining yourself: what have you actually got on the level of views and knowledge? You should not fall into this field of idle talk, and take it for the true seed of entering the Way. Think on it deeply.

The road that goes upward — those who draw near to it are few. If one is not truly a wondrous man, one can never go in single-file with a straight blade. This matter is by no means something that the cleverness and nimbleness of the world can piece together; nor is it the "thou" and "verily" of worldly views and knowledge that may be taken as a wondrous awakening; nor is it the memorizing and reciting of the ancients' dark sayings and wondrous words that may be taken as one's own understanding. One must truly inquire and truly investigate, until it flows out from one's own breast; only then does it cover heaven and cover earth.

If you have the will to inquire, you need only spit out all your former views and knowledge. Even the characters of the "Great Man" and "Kong Yiji" primers are not permitted to remain in your breast. Spit until all is clean and bare, until not a single thing remains; let go and let go again, until you reach the place where there is nothing left to let go. Only then is it the hour of taking it up. At that time you should press your effort; work until you reach the place where you cannot work, standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high — only then is it the hour of gaining strength.

With your mind thus employed, it is like driving a dog to leap a wall: there must come a stretch of light bursting out from within, and only then is it a place of true enjoyment. This is by no means something one reaches by drifting along. If one is not truly a true man with a settled resolve, one cannot arrive here. How many clever and nimble fellows in the world have handed in their articles of surrender in the field of the five desires; the higher sort hand them in on the road of fame and profit — and that is all. How many ever had their own livelihood?

With your faculties, and your firm and solid faith, you already possess the root. This is the rarest thing of all. But if you imitate the lip-drum Chan of the present age, which only supplies talk for a bell, and do not investigate the actual, will you not betray your own spirit? Because you believe this old man in your heart with settled and undoubting certainty, I dare not fail the hope of your turning to me. My former letter was presumptuous; trusting in one who knows me, I did not spare my eyebrows. It was not to strip you bare; I wish you to reach the true actual, and not to fall into the common rank at the doors and thresholds. You say of yourself that you have accepted things under the stick and the shout; this shows well your great strength. But you must know that the ancients did not lightly apply the stick and the shout, and that even accepting is not a thing to be done carelessly.

I pray you, from today on, lay down all views and knowledge; and at the very place where you lay them down, rouse yourself. Then you will see true enjoyment. Because my hope for you is not shallow, I do not spare these garrulous words; and it is precisely because you have this great strength that I lay a thousand-catty burden on you. In your reading, please take up Dahui's letters and look at them; then you will see that this old man does not deceive you with idle words.
To Mu Xiangxuan, Censor

I have long had the wish to rest in old age on Mount Nan. Last winter I came on foot with my staff, but the conditions for a mountain dwelling were not yet met. Lately I have been lodging temporarily east of the lake in Hengyang, which is also an ancient place of the Way. When Master Qin came I learned all about you, sir, and how in recent days you have greatly done the Buddha's work and suddenly opened the eye of gods and men. Hearing it, my joy was beyond measure.

I have often said that the hero-knights of past and present have a stretch of prajñā light that is mostly covered over by worldly conditions; they put all their strength into the doors of fame and wealth, and those willing to set foot on the upward road of their own root and source of life are very rare. Therefore this great matter is the place of final homecoming for a great man. That you, sir, can suddenly turn toward it and look back on fame and career as mere dust and chaff — how I admire you! I regret only that I cannot decide the upward matter together with you, and count this a lack. I hear that you, sir, keep the Vajra Prajñā diligently; I have lately a volume, Resolving Doubts, which I present to you as a gift of Dharma.
Reply to Liu Yushou, Ministry Official

At Wuguan I had the good fortune to enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti; since then our letters have kept in touch, only I have not yet answered your thought of taking refuge. For this I am ashamed. After we parted I entered Mount Kuang and lingered there six years. In the long-zhi month of renxu I set out again for Lingnan, and received the letter you had sent in the intercalary month of xinyou; only in the second month of guihai was I able to open and read it. Such is the delivery of a single letter — how much more so the affinities of many lives in a human life?

The record of your illness that you showed me I read carefully line by line. Though it is the form of illness, in essence it arises in the habit-energy you have investigated; it is not karmic habit. In it I see that your joy is not lacking. But to take it as actual realization is not yet permissible. Moreover, the clear instruction of the Śūraṅgama says that even what comes from true inquiry in Chan concentration is not to be taken as a certificate, and that to take it as a sagely understanding is at once to receive a host of evils — how much more the form of illness? Nevertheless, having passed through this once, you should trust your own mind the more, sweep away your former views and knowledge, and then you need not fear that you will not arrive at the land of peace.
Reply to the Magistrates of Hangzhou

I am ashamed of my own meanness and inferiority, having been a sinner against the Dharma gate; I have drifted on the sea of miasma for more than twenty years, bones wasted and spirit dissolved, with only a breath left. I meant to hide my traces in the remote mountains and end my days in this world. But for the sake of the Dharma gate, and because I had with Master Da a bond of life and death, and grieving that Master Lian's sun of wisdom has set, I came without grudging several thousand li, carrying a petal of incense to mourn. Now I have fulfilled my vow at Shuangjing, and mean to pass the last of winter and then journey to Yunqi; I must take the road by Qiantang and enter the chamber of Vaiśālī.

How could I have expected that you great elders would do me the honor of sending your compassionate command first? I met Master Xuanjin and learned in full the splendor of the Dharma assembly. What good fortune for my remaining years to see such a day again! My gratitude cannot be spoken; I bow down in shame with nowhere to put myself. I respectfully send this thanks. In time I shall reverently receive your censure, to melt away my narrowness and inferiority.
To the Prince of Jing, of Qizhou

I respectfully consider Your Highness the worthy prince: your sagely virtue is Heaven-born, your spiritual root planted in former lives. Within you cherish true compassion; without you manifest as a sovereign. Your body dwells in the toil of the dust, your mind rests in the Pure Land. I am a withered old man of the mountains and forests, and I have looked up to your virtue and admired your manner for many a day. I had judged myself without affinity to receive even a meal's gracious inquiry. Last autumn, as I was wandering about Mount Kuang and about to set out, it happened that the old monk of Guizong brought your princely command. I respectfully received the gift of the fragrant meal; but I was hurrying on pilgrimage and had no leisure to offer thanks. This summer I have returned to Mount Kuang and mean to make it my resting place in old age. Happily my old friend Minister Wang has looked on me with a Dharma eye and wishes to form a society of ten worthies and enter the Lotus Society together, and would have Your Highness as its head. I once asked your attendants to convey this, but I think it did not reach your sagely hearing. Yet Mount Kuang is Vulture Peak, and Qi and Huang are Śrāvastī: how could the Dharma gate leave out Your Highness? I would have it be a golden rampart from first to last.

Now I have received the honor of your messenger and with him your gift of Dharma, and I am deeply moved by your compassionate thoughts. My thanks are beyond measure. And I hear of the death of your heir; I know that Your Highness, bound by the deepest ties of kinship, cannot avoid grief and pain. But the length of a human life is appointed for each; it belongs to former conditions. What is past cannot be kept, and for what is to come we may still hope greatly. How can one injure the nature of the living for the sake of a spirit that cannot be recalled? Here a man of understanding must dismiss it by principle; by no means let deluded thoughts burden your jade person the more. I only hope that the compassion of the Three Jewels may be enough to benefit both the living and the dead. May Your Highness take good care of yourself.
Reply to the Heir of Jing

Since the late king ascended to rule, the affairs of the state have been full of difficulty; Your Highness is young and is only now diligently studying. All matters within and without rest on the single person of the Queen Dowager, and how heavy must her anxiety and toil be? For this I cannot put you out of my mind. Yet you must know how to take care of yourself: restrain grief and lessen vexation, still the mind with quiet, govern those below with kindness, and so secure Heaven's favor. By no means grieve to excess, but comfort the hopes of the many. As for reciting the Buddha's name, chanting sūtras, and bowing in worship, these are your own urgent great matter; and you must not let hardship turn your mind back from them. Set aside this single thought, and there is nothing by which to move the Buddha and the gods to protection; only utter sincerity can touch Heaven.
Reply to Weng Zhaoji of Wuxi, Director of Studies

Your resolve for the Way is genuine and pure; you are a model of human relations. I pray you open and instruct those who come to learn, and make it your highest aim that they truly inquire and truly investigate and do not fall into the gate of light and shadow. On the whole, if the school of sagely learning can truly inquire into the work of the Chan gate, then only will it have the actual. And the habits of recent times mostly love to talk of the brisk and awakening phrases of the Chan school; this is a great abuse and has misled no few. Because they remain on the lips, they are not true views and knowledge. As for the three sūtras — the Laṅkāvatāra, the Śūraṅgama, and the Vajra — they reveal the highest and foremost truth; to look on them as mere words and letters is not the true eye. I pray you give them your mind and open and investigate them constantly; then you will gain the true road's head. Since in the final age there are no clear-eyed men, it is on these that we rely for confirmation.
To Wen Ziyu

I think of your mind set on birth and death, as urgent as if your head were on fire. In the mud of the five desires, if one is not so firm and bold and fierce as this, it is truly hard to pull the root out at once. If amid the heat of affliction a single thought of coolness arises, that is a lotus born in fire. But I regret that your constitution is weak and soft, though the strength of your will and the firmness of your bones are there; only your physical power is not full. You are often ill, and do you know the source of this illness? Other men's illnesses arise from worldly greed and delusion; your illness arises from greed and delusion for the sake of the Way. The illnesses differ, but as illness they are one.

You are full of ardor to escape birth and death; you take escaping the net of dust as escaping birth and death, not knowing that leaving the net of deluded thought is truly escaping birth and death. Moreover, the grace of your parents cannot yet be requited at once; if you take going far away as requital, then you only add to your parents' grief, and so bring suffering back upon your kin. What requital is that? Because you cannot get free, you sit day and night in foolish deluded thought, thinking your will is not fulfilled; and so the Way is not yet done, while the sprout of suffering already grows. Is this not great folly? You should think to yourself: deluded thought is the root of birth and death. Right in your illness, see that this deluded thought has no root or base at all; then in thought after thought you will at once pull out birth and death. Just by sitting thus you advance in this Way; the Dharma body grows daily stronger and the mind-ground daily clearer, and you are freed without waiting to be free. This old decayed one is moved by your faith and cannot forget you from time to time. Hearing that your illness is not yet settled, I send this to comfort you.
To Jin Shengwu, Censor

In former times, hero-knights who bore the talent to order the age knew only of building merit and establishing a career that would not decay; how should they know the work that truly does not decay? Because they did not penetrate what they originally possess, but cast themselves away and followed others, their merit was not always accomplished; and even when accomplished, it was not always imperishable. Even if they had an empty name handed down to later ages, the name survives to no profit, and dark karma follows it. That cause and effect are plain to men's eyes and ears — the generals and ministers of old mostly fell into this. Who among them could be like the great elders Pei, Zhang, Bai, and Yang, who were in the world and yet beyond it?

Hence one knows that there are those who first possess the truth of the nature and then push its surplus into fame and career; and there are those who, having accomplished their merit, withdraw their persons and return to the root in the nature and life. Though early and late differ, in their transcendence and solitary attainment, with which the world cannot compare, they are one. You, sir, at the very time of having accomplished your merit and withdrawing, can at once lay down all conditions and quietly give your mind to the ground of the one real. What is called the highest joy in oneself would not be exchanged for nine tripods. Are you not a great hero-knight?

Only press your effort right where you have laid things down. Lay down until you reach the place where there is nothing left to lay down, and of yourself you will not be bound by the karma of birth and death. Even in practicing the one gate of the Pure Land, the most essential thing is to lay down defiling conditions, and only then does pure karma succeed. Yet to seek the Pure Land at the very place of laying down is to exchange that for this, a method of bartering. The place of the Way at Yunqi has pure rules and solemn stillness, like a vajra ring. I wish only that the assembly be of one mind and practice according to the teaching; then Master Lian's Dharma body sits majestically on the lion seat. Only let the great benefactors who protect the Dharma constantly add their blessing, to increase your diligence. What more is there to say?
To Yan Tianchi, Grand Secretary

After I returned to the mountain I already sent a full report, to comfort your compassionate thoughts. The site I chose for my mountain dwelling is the most secluded and lovely. With much effort I cut thatch for a few rafters, and after the middle of the tenth month it was done; I have been settled in it nearly three months. At the year's end all is at its end, and there is nothing but the piled snow of a thousand peaks and the pine waves of ten thousand gorges filling the ear and dazzling the eye, while a white-haired old man with tangled beard and hair sits there listlessly, wrapped in his robe, round the stove, burning tree stumps, so far off that he does not know there is a human world, and the human world does not know that within heaven and earth there is such a creature. The toil of accumulated kalpas can be washed away at a stroke — how much more the steaming heat and poisonous fog of twenty years? I think that when you, elder layman, hear this, you will surely clap your hands once.
To Wang Jihe

You say that lately you are daily more slack and have no power of diligence. This is the clarity of self-knowledge. The sūtra says: know it to be an empty flower, and there is no turning about. Since you know it as slackness, then surely you will not be turned by slackness. The ancients said: when the mind does not join and merge with worldly feeling, that is true diligence.

I hear lately that you are reading with Yuanchu in the mountains of Dongting, far removed from the objects of the dust, with the six senses having nothing to lean on, placed amid the vast and boundless cold waves of thirty-six thousand qing, as if sitting inside a great perfect mirror, and moreover talking of the non-dual with a worthy friend. In such a place, where is there room for slackness? I fear only that deluded thought does not rest, like dreaming in broad daylight, and you give rise to your own upside-down views.
To Gu Luchu, Magistrate

You have a natural bone of the Way and were endowed with a measure that transcends the dust; nurturing your simplicity in the mountains and forests, you may well be called lofty. But as for the root and source of the nature and life, the one stroke that transcends birth and death, it seems you have not yet given it your mind. Your faculties are already complete; what is lacking is a good teacher to whet and polish you — it may simply be that the season and conditions have not yet come.

I have chosen a dwelling south of Mount Kuang, below the Seven Worthies Peak, facing the Five Elders and bowing to one another in the clouds, breathing in and out Lake Pengli. Wave-light and cloud-shadow are no less than Lake Tai, and though flowers and fruit cannot rival Dengwei, the seclusion surpasses it. I am fortunate to lodge here in leisure as an old man at rest, and I wish to imitate the old affair of Huiyuan at Donglin: I would invite the lofty worthies of the realm to join in the pact of the Lotus Society. If you are willing to give your mind to this, I hope you will arrange with friends of like mind that each set out his vow; and when the place of the Way is built, then another day we shall return as a long-absent guest returns home, grow old together amid the mist and rosy clouds, and go together to the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Is this not the highest of affinities? If you would indeed graciously act as our forerunner, there is no need for me to wag my tongue.
To Yu Suxin, Ministry Official

Formerly I met you at Dongchan, and beheld your countenance of the Way and heavenly form, generous and solid and weighty. I knew in my heart that you were a man of power. What I regretted for you was that you had the vessel of the Way but had not heard the Way, and I feared that when the great matter came, the man would not overcome Heaven. If you do not rouse a true and genuine faith and apply your refined effort within the Buddha-Dharma, plumbing deeply the study that transcends birth and death as the place of the real, then the mouth and ear of the world are none of them the ultimate ground.

For true practice beyond the world, there is no sūtra like the Śūraṅgama; for the wonder of responding to the world, there is nothing that surpasses the one book, the Dao De Jing. I pray you rouse your faith early and apply your strength here; in time you will have a place of your own attainment.
To Xiong Zhigang, Censor

Formerly, passing through Wuchang, I had the chance to gaze on your bright countenance, and you graciously did not disdain me but treated me generously, so that I ate my fill of fragrant rice and deeply received your excellent words. You spoke at length of that spirit of yours in Liaodong: majesty that reaches the barbarians, a spirit that would swallow the Hu, laying down weapons of war, and cowing the strong foe like an infant. Every matter came wholly out of the great treasury of light and the vajra mind. Hearing it, I could not help but feel a glow in every pore. I privately said: a bodhisattva manifesting the body of a magistrate, settling the realm and bringing peace to the state, is all spiritual play. I had heard such words before; now I see the man. If one becomes a Buddha with such a mind, one may truly leap straight in — truly a bold and fierce true man!

After we parted, your bright presence appears from time to time in the mirror of my mind. Lately I hear that you have quietly given your mind to the Buddha's work; this is another step beyond the world. There is an old saying: the heart has sorrows beyond number in a lifetime; if not in the gate of emptiness, where shall they be dissolved? This gate of emptiness is truly the place where a hero-knight steps back. If you are willing to set your body down in it, and with the fire of great wisdom melt away your temper and spirit, then cherish this unexcelled sharp weapon, call it your master, lean on it as your long sword that supports heaven, and grasp the eye of heaven and earth; then one day your spiritual powers, looking back at what you were before, will be a single spit. This is truly what I hope. Do you, in your loftiness, have such a mind?
To Cai Wuyue, Prefect

Formerly I was fortunate to have the affinity to meet your bright countenance once, and at once you graciously sealed my mind in the Dharma gate. You undertook to be a protector of the Sixth Patriarch; though the icchantikas made obstacles, the vajra seed is already unground. Afterwards, the karma of Caoxi was likewise devoured by the lion-worm, so that my original vow was crossed, and it became a koan for the future. I too shook myself free and withdrew. Before long I received grace and crossed the mountain pass; at first I meant to rest in old age on Mount Nan but did not succeed, and so made the journey to Shuangjing to finish Master Da's unfinished karma. In the monasteries I passed through, everywhere your mind-light shone; and as for the one stroke that goes upward in the Chan school, all without exception pushed you forward as foremost. Among the magistrates of the Dharma's decline, one who can truly inquire and apply his strength as you do cannot be counted on a second hand. I think that in these years your practice on the ground has become true; you must be passing the barriers with a swing of the arm, at ease wherever you meet conditions, and all illusions have become lamps of prajñā wisdom lit by you.
Reply to Wang Yufan

When Master Tan came, I received the honor of your letter. You fix your heart earnestly on the one matter of birth and death, and have roused this great mind; this is very rare. But you say that Buddha-recitation has successive stages, and you wish to seek the teaching of sudden awakening. This is the tasty fare that the scholars and officials who study Buddhism in recent times love to eat; it is not the medicine that answers the illness. It comes of not truly having a mind set on birth and death, but merely talking of dark and wondrous principles. To speak of birth and death with the mouth while not even knowing what the root of birth and death is — the root of birth and death is precisely the various deluded thoughts of our daily use: self and other, like and hate, greed, anger, and delusion, and all the afflictions and karma. If a single thread of this karma is not cut, it is the root of birth and death.

Now you say you want to inquire into Chan, awaken suddenly, and finish with birth and death. Please measure it yourself: can you in a single thought cut off the afflictions of kalpas past, as one cuts through a tangled skein? If you cannot cut off affliction, then even if you can awaken suddenly, it becomes demonic karma. How can this be taken lightly? The sudden awakening of the patriarchs of the past also came out of gradual practice and accumulated merit over many lives. Therefore the one stroke of sudden awakening seems easy when spoken of, but is in truth difficult. Without twenty or thirty years of a dead mind at work, how can you awaken suddenly in a single thought amid the heat of affliction? It also depends on knowing what your own faculties are like.

As for the one gate of Buddha-recitation, the world does not know its wonder and looks on it as shallow and near. In truth, every step treads on solid ground. Why? Because since we were born, thought after thought we have climbed after deluded objects and made the karma of birth and death; never once has a single thought turned the light back to illumine our own mind; never once has a single thought been willing to cut off affliction. Now if you can truly turn the mind of deluded thought into Buddha-recitation, then in thought after thought you cut off affliction. If in thought after thought you can cut off affliction, then in thought after thought you escape birth and death. If this one thought is undisturbed, then at the approach of death evil karma dissolves, the Buddha's realm appears before you, and in a single thought you go with the Buddha to be born in the Pure Land, forever transcending birth and death and ascending to the ground of non-retrogression. It is said: if one but sees Amitābha, why worry that one will not awaken? Why then must one discuss sudden and gradual? Why bother about the three grades and the nine grades? It is like passing the imperial examination in the world: even the last name on the list will do — why must one be the very first? If it be as you say, and one's Chan inquiry is thorough from head to tail, then the five turbid realms and the ten directions are all the Pure Land. Those words are very rousing. But I fear you cannot be like that, and would you not then deceive yourself in this life and fall again into the long kalpas of birth and death?

If you can truly keep the one thought of Buddha-recitation unmoved and the one mind undisturbed, it has a better landing place than Chan inquiry. In the end it all lies in the one thought being genuine and keen. But Chan inquiry requires that the worldly mind die completely, and does not allow a single deluded thought; while Buddha-recitation uses pure thought to turn defiled thought, and uses thought to remove thought — it is a method of bartering, and easier for our faculties. In truth, when mind after mind recites the Buddha and mind after mind is not darkened, the wondrous joy of that mind cannot be spoken of. Please try it. I hope you will not take this old decayed one for a teacher of inferior understanding. These are not deceitful words; may your mind forgive them. The teaching of the three grades of the Pure Land I once set out fully in my Discourses on the Pure Land Assembly. Do not be confused by false teachings; please read it carefully. I need not say more.
Thanks to Wu Shugu, Chancellor

I have just received your letter and learn that you, sir, from time to time seal your mind with the Laṅkāvatāra. Formerly Zhang Fangping happened to obtain a copy of it and it seemed to be a manuscript in his own hand from a former life; this too is an old possession in your breast. But this sūtra's text is perilous and its meaning deep, and I have not measured myself, but have presumptuously made notes on it, unable to bring out a ten-thousandth part. You ask why this sūtra does not establish a ninth consciousness. The reason is that the Buddha taught according to faculties, and his teaching has the provisional and the real. When he first appeared in the world, the vessels to be transformed were not yet ripe and could not bear the great, so he provisionally taught the inferior faculties of the small vehicle that the six consciousnesses and the three poisons are the root of birth and death; even the eight consciousnesses he kept secret and did not dare to teach. Only after thirty years, when the faculties had gradually ripened, did he teach consciousness-only, taking the eight consciousnesses as the root of delusion and awakening, birth and death. Still fearing they would not believe in the buddha-nature, he established beyond the eight a further ninth, called the stainless consciousness, to draw them onward. This too is not yet the complete meaning of the great vehicle. After this, seeing that the faculties were ripe, he taught the Laṅkāvatāra, pointing directly to the storehouse of consciousness as the tathāgatagarbha, as the sudden teaching of the great vehicle. This sūtra does not establish the successive stages and names of practice and realization; it only requires that one understand the one thought's non-arising and at once be identical with the Buddha's substance. Therefore although the sūtra has all manner of words, they all break the illness of attachment to words in the outsiders and the small vehicle; it only teaches one to be free of words and deluded thought and at once to tally with the original mind. Hence when Bodhidharma came from the West he took this sūtra as the mind-seal; it is entirely unlike the teaching of the other sūtras. You need only look at the one phrase in the sūtra — the storehouse of consciousness is the tathāgatagarbha — and that is the ultimate and final principle; there is no need to seek a ninth consciousness as a real dharma. On the whole this sūtra wants only freedom from words and deluded thought as the work of entry; open the scroll and at once all is not so — that is the correct command of the Buddha and Patriarchs. Such are my presumptuous thoughts. I pray you, sir, give them your attention.
Reply to Ruan Danyu, Prefect

Last year I heard that you had hung up your cap and returned east, and my joy and comfort were beyond measure. A bodhisattva's saving of living beings is indeed his original practice; but in the age of the kalpa's turbidity, when living beings' defilement is heavy, even Śākyamuni could not help knitting his brow — how can one fulfill one's vow-power to the end? White clouds over quiet mountains and the pure blessing of later years count for more than that. If you cultivate pure karma with care and so take long leave of the realm of endurance, that is again the highest affinity for a true man.
The Dream Wanderings of Elder Hanshan, Volume Eighteen
To Wang Xingdong, Censor

After we parted in the winter of renzi, the following year I was gravely ill and nearly died and came to life again. By winter I had crossed the pass to Mount Nan. At first I had meant to rest in old age there, but the conditions did not allow it; and since Master Da had koans unfinished, in the summer of bingchen I made the journey to Wu and Yue. I sought news of you but could not get any. First I went to Mount Lu for the summer retreat; seeing how secluded and lovely it was, I formed the resolve to end my days there. When Master Da's affair was finished, in the fifth month of dingji I returned to Mount Kuang, and divined a spot below the Five Milk Peak in the south of the mountain, one hill and one gully, enough for my remaining years. The conditions for building it all depended on the protectors of the Dharma, and now I am happily settled. What I longed for twenty years I have attained only in my declining years; one may know that the blessing of mountains and forests in a human life is not easily got.

Last summer, if you had come — you graciously sent a letter from afar — I learned only then that you were at home in mourning for a parent. I reckon the mourning will soon be over and your entry to the capital may be looked for. When your boat passes Luoxing, and you lift your head to the cloudy mountain a single lowing of an ox away, I look day and night for the affinity of a fine meeting. I often think of the Dharma in Lingnan: for a thousand years it has been so, and though this old decayed one has not greatly revived it, I relied on your entering the society; for a time the company flourished, with Feng and Long and the two students as its leaders, and every man was presentable. Alas, those two have followed one another in death, and this Way is thin and few. I rely only on your power of bearing it. But I cannot long deal with the company; scattered without a leader, it is greatly to be grieved. I did not think that rise and decline could be so swift.

You are richly endowed by Heaven, and my only regret is that you have not been able to enter deeply into the Dharma gate. Then though you have the heart to protect the Dharma, as for the one stroke of decisively letting go, it seems you have not yet broken through. Hence you still have boundaries between worldly dharma and Buddha-Dharma. If you could open wide the double gates so that inside and outside are perfectly clear, like the sun and moon hung in the mid-heaven, then how could the robe and bowl of Caoxi be left to rot? If a man of your great strength does not rouse the unsurpassed bodhi mind, then in the great darkness there will be no torch of wisdom at all. This old decayed one is old; my remaining days are few. I constantly think of this stretch of karma and grieve over it deeply. Will you take thought of it? Master Xiu has shut himself in a death retreat on the summit of the Golden Wheel Peak, and there is much hope in it. Ruoxing is now staying in the mountain for the time being to work at the rattan vines and to be led into the gate of wisdom. If in another day these two gain you as a protector of the Dharma and greatly spread this Way, then though this old decayed one die, he will not perish, and the affinities of many kalpas will not have been in vain. What more is there to say? Ten thousand li are as a face-to-face meeting. Do but consider it.
Reply to Chen Wuyi, Ministry Official

Dwelling in the mountains, I am daily farther from the world; yet whenever I hear of the times, my heart is alarmed and the pain pierces my five inward organs. I did not think it would change to this. With a young sovereign standing alone and government issuing from many gates, it is what is called too many physicians making the pulse chaotic; no wonder it is so. Even Bian Que would be at a loss. What is to be done?

The overturned cart ahead is a warning; for now one should only walk warily and keep watch, to firm the fence and nurture the vital force — that is the best policy. To bind oneself anxiously to a broken vessel and insist that it be made whole, and to prize a tasty, pleasing satisfaction, is what is called: the illness does not kill the man, but the doctor does. Beyond this, what other art is there? For a time the court has indeed many noble men; but even if they can take up the classic and feel the pulse, I fear that with many and strange prescriptions they may not be able to bring off a cure.

Your mourning will soon be over and you will at once go out to fill a post. Do not make order or chaos the test of whether to act. It is said: when the great fire burns, this land of mine is at peace. Worldly affairs are like a game of chess: the player is confused, but if there is a clear-eyed one looking on, he may point out one move and win the whole game — what need is there to be in the game? But you should not roll up your sleeves into it and make the players weary of you. This is what our Buddha taught: the precious thing is to practice with skill and expedient means. What do you say?

You show me that your solitary clarity appears from time to time, but that you do not take it up bravely. If you say it appears, that is the clarity of self-knowledge; if you say you do not take it up bravely, that is that your self-belief does not reach. Yet its appearing is appearing in thought after thought — how could it be only from time to time? Only see through to the fact that in the very place where it appears there is originally not a single thing; then what appears before you in thought after thought is your original face. Press on in thought after thought, and thought after thought is unborn; the whole substance appears, and what is there then of taking up or not taking up? Because the man himself does not believe in a single thought, he gives rise to the mind that thinks there is something else; therefore he misses it face to face, and yet says he does not take it up bravely. The illness lies in the mind that seeks elsewhere. All who turn toward the Way go astray through this. You need only see through the unborn right at the place where a single thought appears. If unborn, then originally there is nothing; and so, far back from the beginningless, a single thought has never shifted, and from now on it is only this single thought — what else is there to seek? Since there is only this single thought, who is there to take it up?

The Sixth Patriarch said: as for this matter, one may do it even with a sword whirling in battle array. I pray you truly believe in this mind and see through to the place where thought after thought appears; then thought after thought you will be diligent, and thus every place is a field of great liberation. What then is the division of order and chaos? Because meeting face to face is hard, I have unwittingly leaked all this out.
Reply to Cao Nengshi, Judicial Commissioner

I have long admired the loveliness of Mount Kuang, and only in my declining years have I gone there. In the year bingchen I climbed this mountain once, and knew that there was a great magistrate and good teacher to be a banner protecting the Dharma; and when I read the appeal for the Dragon Canon, my heart bowed to one who had the spiritual power of Vimalakīrti to cut off and take a whole great chiliocosm. Soon after I cut thatch at Wuru, meaning to rest in old age. Below the peak it leans on the Seven Worthies at the edge of heaven, and gazes at the Five Elders in the clouds, right at the brow and lashes, to be the protector of my monastery gate.

Master Zang toils and struggles for the place of the Way, never resting his feet, and is glad without ever wearying. And your reverence has a great vow-power and will establish a Dharma feast; this is a vast and great affinity for Mount Kuang. But it requires that you come in person in your Dharma body to this place, and only then can the great Dharma drum be sounded. Otherwise, how can one dung-sweeping ascetic give fearlessness to the cloud-borne sea of the assembly of the ten directions? In this vast heart you must surely establish this rare thing.
Reply to Xu Mingheng, Minister of War

Day after day you have graciously condescended to visit this wild mountain; at one meeting the light of wisdom stood out alone, clear within and without like an ice jar or a jade mirror — truly a man of prajñā, not one whose good roots were perfumed and cultivated in only one or two lives. And when I heard the subtle words you let fall, a single stretch of vajra mind-ground issued as a loyal liver and righteous gall: you have only the one thought of loyalty to the sovereign and love of the realm, and no longer know that there is any reckoning of body or household. Truly you have come riding on the power of a vow to save suffering living beings, manifesting indeed as a magistrate and doing the Buddha's work.

You have sent your virtuous words from afar, and I know that your Dharma body is much afflicted. You say that your mind is strong but your bones weak. This is so in a body with outflows: it is originally floating and brittle, and the principle is surely so. Consider this body of blood and flesh: it is originally a congelation of deluded thought, steaming and suffusing in thought after thought; so when care and regulation are slightly amiss, it shows no gratitude at all. And moreover the outer desires that press upon it add to the root of illness. Only the Buddha alone, purely with the vajra mind-ground, transforms it in thought after thought, and so makes this body wholly firm, and his relics are indestructible.

I have heard that the truth of the sagely Way is used to govern the self, and its dregs to govern the world and the state. This is a teaching of root and branch. But now your will is to benefit others; first establish the root. Let what you nourish be firm and deep, and afterwards forget the body in the work. Laozi said: put yourself behind and you come first; set yourself outside and you survive. There must be a Way in this.

You, sir, have a great will and a great vow; it must be that the mind is great and the body fine, and only then can it be. Here there is something to be guarded within, and matters outside to test it by; then you will gradually enter a fair realm, as when building a tower, one must first lay its foundation. My foolish wish is that from today you rouse your mind and simply hold to one mantra — either Cundi or the Vajra Ucchuṣma — keeping it in your mind, never forgetting it throughout the six periods of day and night. In time a strong and resolute spirit will be perfumed and issued of itself, and you will be strong without forcing yourself to be. Knowing your lofty wisdom and your deep and solid faith, I have dared to speak wildly.
